titleStmt.title: Cluster-Based CAN with Enhanced Transmission Capability for Vehicle Networks

analytic.title: Cluster-Based CAN with Enhanced Transmission Capability for Vehicle Networks

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Controller area network (CAN) is widely used in automotive control systems as standard networks. However, the bandwidth limitation can not fulfil the communication requirement from increasing number of electronic components in vehicles. We propose to divide the nodes on the CAN buses into clusters. Communication cycles include the intra and inter communication time for transferring messages inside and between the clusters. The proposed method is called ClusterCAN which is a cyclic communication method based on CAN. ClusterCAN can transmit numerous messages simultaneously under proper clustering to enhance throughput. We provide the design concept of the bus segmentation and communication cycle for parallel transmission for the proposed ClusterCAN. Furthermore, the worst case response time analysis of the ClusterCAN is derived and used in the simulations. From the experimental results, the schedulable messages increase 50% and 75% under two and three clustering groups with the fixed inter connection ratio (10%) compared to the normal CAN.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The number of electronic devices in vehicles has increased to replace the mechanical and hydraulic parts for years. Using the electronic system reduces the weight and cost of vehicles as well as provides better control. All these electronic components need an efficiency way to exchange information, and controller area network (CAN) is a low cost, reliable, flexible, and extensible communication protocol.

The bandwidth of CAN is limited to 1Mb/s that can not fulfil the future requirement such as driver assistance, chassis management and powertrain management [1]. To resolve the bandwidth problem, a protocol with higher data rate such as Flexray or a system with multiple CAN buses must be used. The cost of higher data rate communication protocol is higher than the CAN, and the cost is very important in manufacturing industry. Thus, the multiple CAN buses design is a relatively acceptable solution. The Volvo XC90 uses two different speed CAN buses for powertrain, chassis and body electronics. Furthermore, the BMW 7 series even adopts four CAN buses for different subsystems. The detail network architecture of these multiple CAN buses systems can be found in [2].

However, the multiple CAN buses may be not enough for the increasing data rate [1]. Gateways are required to connect multiple CAN buses, and the delay caused by multiple gateways is unacceptable. Also the gateway often become the bottleneck of the system due to the priority-based network access method and the limited resource like buffer size [3].

There are some researches try to improve the throughput of CAN. Overclocking of CAN [4] increases the bit rate for the single-writer-allowed zones, and the throughput can be doubled. However, the overclocking method need to redesign the communication controller, and is not compatible with original communication controllers. The other proposed method to improve the throughput is CAN+ [5] which can increase the data rate up to 16 times. Although the CAN+ can transfer 16 times information than the normal CAN by a frame, but if the data size of single frame is not big enough, the throughput improvement can be limited.

To enhance the throughput of CAN buses, we propose to divide the nodes on the CAN buses into clusters. Messages are transferred inside and between the clusters during the intra and inter communication time. We call the proposed method as ClusterCAN which is a cyclic communication method based on CAN. ClusterCAN can handle numerous messages at the same time as long as clustering the nodes properly. Moreover, this method can be implemented by adding some segmentation blocks to the network, and the well designed communication controller can be used without modification.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II provides the overview of the CAN. Section III describes the concept of ClusterCAN including bus segmentation, communication cycle and timing analysis. Section IV provides experiments to discuss the throughput improvement of ClusterCAN. Finally, section V offers conclusion.

div.head: II. CONTROLLER AREA NETWORK(CAN)
div.p: CAN, developed by Robert Bosch GmbH [6] in the 1908s, is a widely used bus communication protocol that is eventtriggered, robust, and low cost. This protocol is mostly used in the in-vehicle networks between electrical control units (ECU). It is also adopted for embedded networks, machine control, factory/building automation, and medical electronics. nodes. Each standard CAN data frame requires a unique 11bits identifier (or 29-bits identifier in the extended mode) in the arbitration field to compete with other data frames for obtaining the right to use bus. The control field follows the arbitration field, containing 4-bits data length code (DLC) to describe the length (0-8 bytes) of the data field. After the data field, 15-bits Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) and 2bits acknowledgement (ACK) are at the end of the frame. The CRC is used to check the bit errors inside the data frame by the receivers. The ACK field is for the receivers to send a dominant bit to inform the sender that they have validated the received bits.

div.head: A. Frame Format
div.p: The maximum transmission time of a data frame can be increased by the stuffing bits. The equation of the maximum transmission time C m for the message m including stuffing bits and inter frame is given by Eq. ( 1), proposed by [7]. The C m contains the number of data bytes (s m ) and the bit time (τ bit ) for a standard data frame is shown below. The number 55 is the bit number of a frame exclude the data field, and the number 10 is for a data byte.

div.head: B. Response Time Analysis
div.p: The bus arbitration on CAN bus is based on message priorities, so the message response time is not deterministic. Response time analysis can provide a mathematical method to find the bound of a response time for each message. These bounds, also called the worst case response time, can be compared with deadline of each message to determine whether the system is schedulable. The original worst case response time analysis was proposed by Tindell [8], [9], later the flaw was discussed and the fix is proposed by [7]. The worst case response time of message R m for the message m can be made up of three elements as Eq. ( 2). The Subscript m means a specific target message that we want to analysis.
div.formula: R m = J m + W m + C m . (2
div.p: First, the queuing jitter (J m ) means the longest time between the triggered event and start of the sending task (ready to be sent on the bus). Second, the queuing delay (W m ) means the longest time that the message can be queued in the CAN controller due to the busy bus.
div.formula: W n+1 m = max(B m , C m ) + ∀k∈hp(m) W n m + J k + τ bit T k (3)
div.p: The first term corresponds to the value of the maximum blocking time by lower priority messages B m and the push through interference due to the previous instance of the same message C m . In the other words, a lower priority message or a older but same priority message can be just started the transmission, hence W m must consider the maximum value of B m and C m . The second term corresponds to the queuing delay caused by the higher priority message sets hp(m) composed by the messages with higher priority than message m. T k is the period of the message k, and J k is the queuing jitter of the message. The numerator inside the ceiling function means the longest time before the transmissions of message m.

div.head: III. CLUSTERCAN
div.p: In order to overcome the bandwidth limitation of a single CAN bus and unacceptable multiple gateway/bridge delay when using multiple CAN buses, we propose a new communication architecture, called ClusterCAN, based on the CAN protocol.

In ClusterCAN, the original bus can be partitioned periodically into several sub-bus which can be used simultaneously. System designer can cluster the highly correlated nodes together into groups and set a proper communication cycle fitting the communication requirement.
We present the ClusterCAN architecture, including bus segmentation, communication cycle, and timing analysis in this section.

div.head: A. Bus Segmentation
div.p: CAN is a broadcast bus, which means each nodes on the media can receive every signals whether it is required or not. The broadcast bus architecture is simple and widely used in different areas, but it may become the system performance bottleneck due to limited bandwidth, power consumption and long wire delay time.

The traffic between nodes can be seen as the distance between nodes, and nodes with heavier traffic are closer. After collecting all information about the communication we can use the hierarchical clustering method to cluster the nodes into groups. The clustering strategy is recursively finding two most closet clusters and merging them as a cluster. The purpose of clustering is to maximize the message volume of intra groups and minimize the message volume of inter groups.

In the very large scale integration (VLSI) design, segmented bus has been proposed for decades. Partitioning a single bus into several tree-structured segments reduces power consumption and critical delay [10]. Segmented bus can improve not only power and operating speed, but also enables the parallel transmission in different segments [11]- [13].

Segmented buses have been used to detect and recover from bus failures in a CAN system like CAN Kingdom [14] and REDCAN [15]. These two protocols need to partition bus into segments to test the signal paths working or not. The detected node failures and link failures can be avoided through disconnecting the faulty segments, and signal path can still be established on the ring topology.

The basic ideal of clusterCAN is to take the advantage of intra communications that only the adjacent nodes involved. The intra communication signals do not propagate to the whole bus, so the bus segments can be regarded as different buses that have different behaviours such as different signals or different baud rates.

Figure 2 gives three examples of possible topology that segmented CAN network can be established. They are the basic line, stub and tree wiring structure which can be used as a module to build a large system. The bus can be segmented by the segmentation block (symbol S in Fig. 2). The ECU nodes (symbol N ) connected to the bus send broadcast signals to others on the bus. The segmentation block must be able to terminate signals from both sides or be transparent for buses from time to time. This feature enables the parallel transmission on segments and enhances the bus utilization. Besides, the bus length inside a segment is much shorter than that of the whole bus, so it makes the higher operating frequency feasible. The other advantage of using segmented bus is the ability of error suppression which reduces the error propagation from fault segment.

One of the possible segmentation block implementation is the conventional CAN repeater which can be adopted, and the MUXes are added to decide whether the signal can pass through the segmentation block or not. The control signal as the input makes the segmentation block operating in either the transparent mode or the segmented mode. However, the delay of this segmentation block is about 120ns∼250ns which is caused by the transceivers and the glue logic inside [16]. This delay is approximate to the delay of a 24∼50 meter cable (about 5 ns/m), so transmission at 1Mb/s for inter segments signals is not acceptable. If the length of a segmented bus can fit the required length, then the transmission inside the segment can be sent at a high speed because signals do not suffer the segmentation block delay.

The other possible realization to segment bus in the RED-CAN. REDCAN protocol adopts the ring bus with RCM (redundant CAN module). The RCM uses four switches to connect both the right side and the left side cable. Ever single node in the ring bus can be segmented from left, right or totally disabled from the bus. The commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) relay has been used to implement the switch in REDCAN, and the characteristic switching times are around 5 ∼ 10 ms which can be replaced with a solid state relay. The switching time of a solid state relay is in the μs order which is fast enough for the cycle communication proposed later.

div.head: B. Communication Cycle
div.p: As mentioned before, ClusterCAN can transmit different messages on segments at the same time. The closet nodes which communicate frequently are clustered together as groups. However, the nodes in the different groups may need to exchange messages, even though the inter group communication may be lighter than the intra group communication. For this reason, all clusters in ClusterCAN must follow a specific protocol with information about when to separate and when to connect together. This protocol can be implemented as a communication cycle with intra communication time, inter communication time and synchronization message.

Figure 3 shows a communication cycle used in the ClusterCAN whose communication is composed by periodic communication cycles as depicted above. Every node in ClusterCAN has to maintain the same schedule to ensure the correctness of communication. The nodes inside clusters use intra communication time to transmit messages, and the nodes cross clusters can only transmit messages during the inter communication time. To ensure the synchronization of the nodes, the synchronization message should be sent at the beginning of a communication cycle. This message with a specific identify but no data byte is transmitted by the master of the ClusterCAN, and the other slaves use this message as a flag to start a communication cycle. The synchronization messages cause overhead which depends on the communication cycle length. Moreover, both CAN standard and extended frame format can be used in the communication cycle.

div.head: C. ClusterCAN Timing Analysis
div.p: To calculate the worst case response time when using ClusterCAN, the communication cycle overhead due to the interleaving of intra and inter communication time must be considered. In the worst case, suppose the message is an intra message and arrives just after the end of the intra communication time, then the message must wait until the next intra communication time. The communication cycle overhead depends on the message type, and suffers from the synchronization message. The Eq. ( 4), and Eq. ( 5) correspond the communication cycle overhead of intra and inter messages.
div.formula: h intra = W n m T c (T inter + C s + C m )(4)
h inter = W n m T c (T intra + C s + C m )(5)
div.p: T c is the period of communication cycle. For the worst case, the ceiling function means that message suffers at least one overhead which is sum of either intra or inter communication time (T intra or T inter ), synchronization overhead (C s ) and the maximum transmission time of this message (C m ). The intra communication time and synchronization time are not allowed to transmit the inter message because they are reserved for intra messages or synchronization task. The maximum transmission time of a message need to be included when the message can not be sent because the time is not enough to finish the transmission before the end of its usable communication time.
Consequently, the worst case queuing delay in Eq. ( 3) must be modified. Define a function β(m) ∈ [Intra, inter] that represents the transmission type of a message m that is either intra or inter.

div.head: IV. SIMULATION RESULTS
div.p: In this section, we investigate how the throughput can be improved by the ClusterCAN and compared to the normal CAN and CAN+ in terms of schedulable percentage for a set of CAN messages. Scedulable means that messages can be transmitted before their deadline.

div.head: A. Traffic Test for Communication Cycle Overhead
div.p: As previously mentioned, the worst case queuing delay increases due to a communication cycle overhead (h intra or h inter ). For each test case in the simulation, we generate 1000 random messages sets to be transmitted in both intra and inter communication time. Each message set contains a number of messages that meet specific bus utilization ranges in steps of 5%. The number of data bytes (1∼8 bytes) for each message is chosen from a uniform random distribution. Message period is chosen from a range(eg. 2ms-12ms) according to a uniform random distribution. Message deadlines are equal to their periods, and message jitter are set to zero. In each case, a 500 K/bits transmission rate and the standard data frame format is used.

To calculate the worst case response time, deadline minus jitter monotonic priority ordering (D-JMPO) is used which means a message with a shorter deadline has a higher priority. Schedulable messages have the worst case response time (R m ) which is less than their deadlines, and a schedulable message set has all its messages schedulable. The individual bus utilization for a schedulable message is defined as the maximum transmission time (C m ) divided by the transmission period (T m ). The bus utilization of a schedulable message set is the sum of individual bus utilization. When the minimum message period is close to the communication cycle overhead (the worst case blocking time), the bus utilization become saturate. For each minimum message period, we find the maximum bus utilization that we can inject the maximum number of schedulable messages into the bus. In the other words, the maximum bus utilization represents the traffic that can be scheduled in certain message period. We assume five different communication cycles as shown on the top of Fig. 4 and 5 with different periods and segmentations for intra or inter messages. Figure 4 shows the maximum bus utilization versus different minimum message period for intra messages. Line 1, line 2 and line 3 have the same inter communication time (1ms), so the minimum worst case blocking time by communication cycle are the same. Consequently, the saturation points of these three lines have the same minimum message period (2ms), and the maximum bus utilizations are increased by the intra communication length. Line 4 and line 5 with higher inter communication time saturate at higher minimum message periods due to the higher intra communication cycle overhead. The maximum bus utilizations of these two lines are the same because of the same intra/inter ratio. The maximum bus utilizations of line 1 is less than line 4 and line 5 even with the same intra/inter ratio since the the shorter communication cycle length that can cause more communication cycle overhead. Figure 5 shows the maximum bus utilization versus different minimum message period for inter messages. similarly, line 1, line 2 and line 3 that have the same inter communication time but different intra communication time are saturated at different minimum message periods. They accord to the intra communication lengths and the maximum bus utilizations depend on the intra communication time.

In conclusion, the communication cycle overhead can dominate the schedulability of message sets. The minimum message period can not be too close to the overhead otherwise the higher priority messages are hard to schedule, and the maximum bus utilization mainly depends on the intra/inter ratio.

div.head: B. ClusterCAN evaluation
div.p: We generate multiple nodes system with grouping communication feature to evaluate the improvement of using Clus-terCAN as network. The nodes are divided into two or three groups in advance, and the connection probability of nodes in the same group is higher than the connection probability crossing groups. A message period between nodes is chosen from the range 5ms to 50ms according to a uniform random distribution.
To choose the intra and inter communication length, the minimum message period must be considered first. The communication cycle overhead for message sets can not be too close to the minimum period.

Figure 6 shows the communication schedulability of 24 nodes clustered into 2 groups with different inter connection rates. The inter connection rate of line 1 is one fifth of the intra connection rate, and the inter connection rate of line 3 is one tenth of intra connection rate. Line 2 and line 4 use the same message sets as line 1 and line 3 respectively to schedule at CAN bus without ClusterCAN. As the figure shows, the traffic in line 1 and line 2 is more than that in line 3 and line 4 because of the higher inter connection rates.

To calculate the throughput improvement, we choose the intra node to node injection probability with the schedulable percentage greater but closet to 90% as the reference point. The injection rate of the reference point for line Figure 7 shows the communication schedulability of 24 nodes clustered into 3 groups with different inter connection rates. There are also two different ratio of inter connection ratio; 20% for line 1 and 2, and 10% for line 3 and 4. The throughput improvements are 33% for line 1 and 86% for line 3, which are improved from 0.3 (line 2) to 0.4 (line 1) and from 0.35 (line 4) to 0.65 (line 4) respectively. As a result of dividing the nodes into more groups, the throughput improvements are more obvious than Fig. 6. At most three messages can be sent at the same time in different sub buses. The performance with more inter communications (line 1) is poorer since the inter communications have to occupy the entire bus which is inefficiency.

Figure 8 shows the schedulability evaluation of 32 nodes with fixed ratio of inter and intra connection rate (10%), and we also compare the results with CAN+ [5]. CAN+ is a backward-compatible CAN protocol with up to 16 times higher data rates. The extra information can be put on the gray zone of the bit time. In our case, the data size is chosen from 1 to 8 bytes, that the CAN+ with 16 times data rates needs only one byte data transmission time of normal CAN for every message. Therefore, the range of theoretical CAN+ throughput improvement is from 46% to 62% derived from Eq. (1). Table I reveals the throughput improvement of Cluster-CAN and CAN+ in different number of groups. Throughput improvements of ClusterCAN increase from 50% to 140% with the increasing number of group. On the other hand, the throughput improvements of CAN+ are between 50% to 100%, which is unrelated to the number of groups. The throughput improvement of CAN+ for the same test message sets of line 1 (2 group) is 100% which is greater than the theoretical value since the resolution of node to node message injection probability is relatively low than other two cases.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we introduced the concept of ClusterCAN which can relieve the bandwidth limitation of CAN. There are two possible bus segmentation method for ClusterCAN as below: Adding some logic to control the conventional repeater for the cut-off mode, but the delay of this method could be unacceptable when using higher data rate. Another method is using the RCM(redundant CAN module) with switches to cut off the bus connections, and the switching time must be considered. Moreover, the nodes on ClusterCAN must maintain a schedule of communication cycle to transmit intra and inter messages at proper time. We also add the ClusterCAN feature to the timing analysis, and give some tests to show how the different configuration of communication cycle can impact the schedulability. In the experimental analysis, the throughput improvements of ClusterCAN were increased from 50% to 140% with the number of group increased from 2 to 4 under the fixed inter connection ratio(10%). In addition, the throughput improvement also dominated by the inter group communication.
